name: Polar form
seoTitle: Polar form Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Polar form: work out magnitude (r) from the real part and the imaginary part. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Polar form calculator turns the real part and the imaginary part into magnitude (r). It suits a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Polar form calculator work?
sections.html:
The Polar form calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports magnitude (r) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the real part (a) and the imaginary part (b).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:

Everything the page asks for and everything it reports, side by side. The roles matter: a value you supply is read from the form, a calculated value is derived from the others and cannot be set directly.

sections.title: The formula behind the Polar form calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Magnitude (r)=(the square root of ((imaginary part (b) ^ 2) + (real part (a) ^ 2)))
Phase (φ)=((imaginary part (b), real part (a)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Real part (a) = 10 and Imaginary part (b) = 10. The calculator returns Magnitude (r) = 14.1421 and Phase (φ) = 45 deg.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Magnitude (r) = 14.1421 and Phase (φ) = 45 deg should be roughly the size you expected from Real part (a) = 10 and Imaginary part (b) = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in degrees, and convertible to any of the 12 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Angle, opening in degrees

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Polar form calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the real part and the imaginary part — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Polar form calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — real part for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Switch the units to the ones you normally use and confirm the numbers are unchanged apart from their label; if they are not, a chip was on the wrong setting.

faq.q: What does the Polar form calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns magnitude (r), derived from the real part and the imaginary part. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Polar form calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the real part and the imaginary part, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter phase (φ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Phase (φ) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Magnitude (r) = 14.1421. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Polar form calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
